claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs lines 29-32: `public async Task<Order> CancelOrderAsync(int orderId)` / `{` / `var order = await repository.FindAsync(orderId)` / `?? throw new KeyNotFoundException($"order {orderId} not found");`. The `??` sits on the method's first statement; the next executable lines are 34-38 (`order.Status = "cancelled";` …). tools/extract-code --tag stage-1 --lines 29-32 reproduces the lesson's block character-for-character.

Whole method (29-38) never reads `order.Status`; it assigns `order.Status = "cancelled"` unconditionally at line 34. No branch exists anywhere in OrderService.cs. ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs catches only KeyNotFoundException(404), ArgumentException(400), Exception(500) — no 409 path in the app at all. Live: order 2 (customer_id 1, status `shipped` in donhang-db) + PATCH /api/v1/orders/2/cancel -> `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, body `{"id":2,"customerId":1,"status":"cancelled",...}`. DB row restored to `shipped` afterwards.
claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-1: DonHang.Domain/OrderService.cs:29-38, DonHang.Api/Middleware/ExceptionHandlingMiddleware.cs:16-30; live lab (donhang-lab, localhost:8080)

claim_verdicts.evidence: Live this session, token from POST /api/v1/auth/login (anh.tran@example.com): `curl -sS -i -X PATCH http://localhost:8080/api/v1/orders/99999/cancel -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"` -> `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found` then `{"title":"Not found","status":404,"detail":"order 99999 not found"}` — byte-identical to the lesson. Source path confirmed: middleware `catch (KeyNotFoundException ex)` -> `WriteProblemAsync(context, StatusCodes.Status404NotFound, "Not found", ex.Message)`, the same WriteProblemAsync that serves the ArgumentException/400 case.

RFC 9110 §15.5.1, verbatim from refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7543-7546: "The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing)." All three examples are defects of the request message itself, matching the claim's "in the request itself".

RFC 9110 §15.5.5, verbatim from refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7589-7591: "The 404 (Not Found) status code indicates that the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists." The claim reproduces both halves.

RFC 9110 §15.5.10, verbatim from refs/rfc/rfc9110.txt:7652-7654: "The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target resource." Same section adds "This code is used in situations where the user might be able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request", which the lesson's shipped-order framing does not contradict.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the `400` bullet ends with a repeatability rule that no claim covers and that RFC 9110 §15.5.1 does not state. 400 is defined only as "the server cannot or will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be a client error" — nothing about a resent request failing identically. It is true of `validating-input`'s empty-items check (a pure input check), not of 400 in general.
issues.quote: `400 Bad Request` — the request itself is invalid, the way `validating-input`'s empty-items check rejects one; sent again unchanged, it fails the same way no matter what it names.
issues.fix: Bind the rule to the example instead of the status class: "…the way `validating-input`'s empty-items check rejects one — that check looks only at the request, so resending the same body gets the same `400`." Then add it to `.meta.json` claims with `version_key: http`, kind `behavior`.

issues.text: Unlisted claim about Problem Details. `versions_used` declares `http_problem_details` but no claim carries that `version_key`, so the one sentence that needs RFC 9457 is unledgered. RFC 9457 §3.1 defines `title`/`status`/`detail` but also `type`/`instance`, and all members are optional; "the same three fields regardless" is a property of Đơn Hàng's `WriteProblemAsync`, not of the format.
issues.quote: Problem Details' shared shape — `title`/`status`/`detail`, the same three fields regardless of which of the three status codes a failure gets.
issues.fix: Rewrite as a statement about this app: "Problem Details' shared shape — every error Đơn Hàng returns carries `title`/`status`/`detail`, whichever of the three status codes it is." Add a claim with `version_key: http_problem_details` citing RFC 9457 §3.1 ("The \"status\" member is a JSON number indicating the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence of the problem"; "Problem details can be used with any HTTP status code").

issues.text: The flowchart starts at `PATCH /orders/id/cancel` and draws a `400` branch that this endpoint cannot produce. `Cancel(int id)` takes no request body, and the `[HttpPatch("{id:int}")]` route constraint makes a non-integer id fall through to the router. Verified live: `PATCH /api/v1/orders/abc/cancel` with a valid token returns `404`, not `400`. The prose then justifies the branch with "an empty item list", which belongs to `POST /api/v1/orders`.
issues.quote:
A[PATCH /orders/id/cancel] --> B{request well-formed?}
  B -->|no| C[400]
issues.fix: Change node A to `A[a write request on an order]` so the diagram is about the three questions, not about this one endpoint; and in the paragraph after it, say the `400` example comes from `POST /api/v1/orders` (empty item list), while the `404` and the cancellation come from `PATCH .../cancel`.

issues.text: Unconditional "always"/"never" about the 400 class, repeated in the five-line summary. RFC 9110 §15.5.1 supports no such guarantee — a 400 can come from something transient (e.g. a rejected request framing) and is not promised to be reproducible. The claim holds only for a deterministic input check like the empty-items one.
issues.quote: while a `400` retried unchanged always fails the same way / Retrying a `404` with a real id succeeds unchanged; retrying a `400` never will
issues.fix: In §6: "…while a `400` from a check like the empty-items one fails the same way every time, because the check reads only the request." In §9 line 5: "…retrying the empty-items `400` unchanged never will, since the request itself was the problem."

issues.text: Ambiguous stem. The question stipulates the order "was deleted overnight" — exactly the condition RFC 9110 §15.5.5 singles out: "the 410 (Gone) status code is preferred over 404 if the origin server knows … that the condition is likely to be permanent." Option `d` is disqualified only by a false premise ("a status code this lesson defines"), not by the HTTP semantics, so a reader who knows RFC 9110 can defend `d` on the merits.
issues.quote: where `99999` was a real order's id yesterday but the order was deleted overnight. What status code fits?
issues.fix: Drop the deletion history from the stem: "…where no order with id `99999` exists in the database — the client is working from a stale list." Keep answer `a`, and reword `d` to "`410 Gone` — the order is gone, so the server should say so permanently" with the explanation: RFC 9110 prefers `410` only when the server knows the removal is permanent; `FindAsync` returning `null` records nothing of the kind, so `404` is what Đơn Hàng can honestly say.

issues.text: The `409` node is drawn as a live branch of the same flowchart as the `404` and `200` branches, both of which were confirmed live. That it does not exist in `CancelOrderAsync` is only disclosed three sentences into the following prose, after a reader has already taken the diagram as a map of the code.
issues.fix: Label the node so the diagram is self-describing: `F -->|yes| G[409 — not implemented yet]`.

issues.text: Self-contradictory wording, repeated in the summary and in quiz q2 option `c`: the id is described as "corrected" and the retry as "unchanged" in the same clause. It also overstates — the same request with a real id can still fail for another reason (a missing token returns `401`; verified live).
issues.quote: You notice this when a `404` retried with a corrected id — one that actually exists — succeeds unchanged
issues.fix: "You notice this when the same request shape, pointed at an id that exists, succeeds — while a `400` resent byte-for-byte does not." Apply the same wording to §9 line 5 and to quiz q2 option `c`.

issues.text: Unlisted claim about a file the lesson never quotes. `repository.FindAsync(orderId)` returning `null` for a missing id is true — `DonHang.Domain/IOrderRepository.cs:7` declares `Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id);` — but that file is not in `example_files` and no claim in the ledger covers it; the ledger's claim 1 covers only the ordering of the two statements.
issues.quote: `repository.FindAsync(orderId)` returns `null` when no order has that id
issues.fix: Add a claim to `.meta.json` with `source_hint` "examples/don-hang @ stage-1: DonHang.Domain/IOrderRepository.cs:7 — Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id)". No prose change needed.

issues.text: `ArgumentException` is used as if I already met it. All I remember from `validating-input` is that a check "turns a bad request into a `400`" — the five-line summary never names an exception type, and section 1 here only says "something outside it catches that exception". So the sentence that ties the two lessons together starts from a name I cannot place, and I cannot tell whether `ArgumentException` is the 400 one or something new.

issues.fix: In "Before you start", name the type once: "…throws `ArgumentException` for an empty item list, and something outside it catches that exception and answers `400`."

The whole `409` idea rests on "already `shipped`", and section 5 then talks about `order.Status`. I can guess, but I am guessing at the one example that explains the third status code.

issues.text: The diagram contradicts itself for me: it starts at "a request fails", yet one of its ends is "succeeds". If the request already failed at node A, how can the last branch succeed? I re-read the box three times before deciding node A must mean "a request arrives".

issues.text: The diagram draws one request walking through three checks, and then the prose takes that reading away: the first question belongs to a different endpoint, the third check does not exist. No node says which endpoint it is about, so while reading I kept asking "which request am I following here?" and had to re-map every box after the first paragraph instead of before it.

issues.fix: Put the endpoint in the boxes so the diagram matches the prose from the start: `C[400 — POST /orders]`, `E[404 — PATCH .../cancel]`, `G[409 — nothing checks this yet]`.

issues.text: I could not choose between `a` (`404`) and `b` (`400`) from the lesson. Core concepts says `400` is for a request with an invalid value — and `validating-input` taught me an empty item list, a value that is well-formed but nonsense, is `400`. `-5` looks exactly like that kind of nonsense value. Nothing in the lesson states the rule that decides it: once the endpoint accepted the value and looked it up, finding nothing is `404` no matter how wrong the value looks.
issues.quote: `-5` is a syntactically valid integer, so the route matches and `CancelOrderAsync(-5)` runs. What status code fits?
issues.fix: Add one sentence to the end of section 4's second paragraph: "An id that is a valid number but matches no order is still `404`, even when the number looks obviously wrong — the request's shape was fine, so the id is the only thing missing."
